source.title: The Geometric Inductive Bias of Grokking: Bypassing Phase Transitions via Architectural Topology

record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking dynamics on modular arithmetic using architectural interventions and the same train/test generalization behavior, rather than reproducing the original intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own training and test accuracy dynamics, generalization epochs, and spectral analyses. Cited results from prior work are not included as rows. Training-set fraction is fixed at 30%; no dataset-size sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own 1-layer transformers on modular addition, multiplication and S5 at a 30% split. Its standard LayerNorm/RMSNorm baselines reproduce the delayed-generalization profile. It then shows that architectural changes (spherical residual stream, uniform attention) remove the delay. It also reports Fourier-ablation and FVE checks, a weight-decay contrast and a normalized-unembedding control. These are its own results bearing on V1, V5, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that two independent interventions each eliminate the memorization phase on cyclic modular arithmetic (addition and multiplication): a fully bounded spherical residual stream, and uniform attention (even with LayerNorm). They note the accelerated models still use Fourier circuits. The same spherical constraint fails entirely on S5, which they read as showing that bypassing the delay depends on alignment between architectural priors and task symmetry. They interpret the result through the norm-separation delay law and attribute the weight-decay friction under the bounded topology to scale-invariance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses small Transformer models and train/test splits on algorithmic modular tasks, with grokking onset and accuracy measurements. Adds spherical-topology and uniform-attention interventions, multiplication and S5 tasks, and spectral analyses; the training-set fraction is fixed at 30%.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with architecture, learning rate, weight decay, attention routing, and task: spherical constraints accelerate cyclic arithmetic but fail on S5; weight decay has little reported effect at learning rate 1 × 10−4 but slows and increases variability at 6 × 10−4; uniform-attention bounded models differ by weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Constraining residual-stream magnitude or replacing learned attention with uniform aggregation removes the grokking delay on cyclic arithmetic. The same spherical constraint prevents generalization on S5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The grokking delay depends on architectural degrees of freedom (residual norm, attention routing) and on their alignment with the task's symmetry, not on the data alone.

record.problems: The evidence uses synthetic algorithmic tasks and a fixed 30% training split, so it does not test the claimed dependence on training-set size or realistic data. Most reported metrics aggregate 10 seeds; uniform-attention S5 results use 5 seeds. The paper reports some circuit measures as aggregate summaries rather than run-by-run comparisons, and the normalized-unembedding control has no numerical result stated.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size; the split is fixed at 30%.
No progress measures are tracked over training, and there is no test of whether they anticipate the jump.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm lazy-to-rich manipulation.
No parameter-norm measurements, no critical dataset size and no ungrokking. The baselines were only run with WD=1.0, so there is no baseline weight-decay contrast.

Only 1-layer transformers are tested, and the comparison is aggregate rather than per-run. It does not test whether different architectures or hyperparameters yield different algorithms (e.g. clock vs pizza).
Adaptive-optimizer instabilities are not controlled (AdamW only, gradients unclipped). StableMax or other floating-point fixes are not tested.

missing.what: L1 normalization (cross-polytope constraint) also failed to generalize on S5; no numbers are given.
missing.locator: Section 5.1, 'From interpretation to design', last sentences

missing.what: A numeric onset or trajectory for the LayerNorm plus normalized-unembedding control on addition.
missing.locator: Section 4.1, 'Empirical Validation of the Bounded Topology'

record.verdict_notes: Single-author preprint with code released. Rows for bounded or uniform-attention conditions were mislabeled 'observed' for V1; they show the delay absent and so limit V1's scope rather than support it. One state per row cannot capture the V5 reading of bounded rows, so it is given in each row's problem text. The paper's norm-separation argument is interpretive: no parameter norms are measured. V7 challenge covers only the logit/softmax-scale side; optimizer artifacts are untested.

versions.untested_parts: The training-set-size dependence is not tested: the reported arithmetic and S5 experiments use a 30% training split, with no comparison across training-set sizes.
The paper analyzes Fourier structure and reports spectral ablations, but does not track gradual circuit formation or test whether continuous progress measures anticipate the accuracy transition.
No non-algorithmic datasets or lazy-to-rich initialization/weight-norm transition are tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.

The paper varies weight decay and reports spectral coherence and grokking outcomes, but does not measure parameter-norm separation, sweep dataset size, or test a critical dataset size or ungrokking prediction.

Fourier structure is assessed across successful configurations, but the paper does not identify and compare a full algorithm separately for every run or test convergence across a broad range of architectures and hyperparameters.

The paper tests whether normalized unembedding alone removes the delay and reports instability associated with weight decay, but does not systematically control adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits.
